The recorder: six drawings, one per path

Every drawing follows the rule of 2026-10-21 (RCD25, RCD28, RCD29): one box per thread, titled by the thread's name, the process as the outer box, generic data structures with their generic operations in each box and on each arrow, and the code name after a tilde. A dashed arrow is a data-structure operation. A solid arrow is control flow. Nothing is drawn that this build does not implement. Each drawing measures zero overlapping lane boxes, zero arrow texts over a box, a lane title or another arrow, zero margins under 0.4 in, and zero overflow. All six drawings are approved (RCD29, RCD30; drawing 2 on 2026-10-22). The text under each drawing follows recorder.md section 2, the design's truth (RCD61).

1. A span or an event: the push, on the calling thread

The calling thread registered at its start and owns one entry of the producers table, with its queue. A seventeenth registration dies. The producer pushes the record into the thread's own queue. One producer, one consumer, no lock while the queue has room. A full queue drops the record, and the thread counts it in its own statistics. While it drops, it builds the drop line itself: the counts, the first and the latest drop time. At its next successful push it queues that line first, so the drop line sits at the hole. If this push crossed half full, the producer sets the writer's wake flag once. The writer sleeps on that flag. Its sleep ends on the flag or after 5 s.

2. The writer's pass: every queue, both pools, the file

The writer is the one consumer of every producer's queue and both pools. It is the one producer of the file. One pass has seven steps, in order, as the header numbers them. Step 1 is the sleep and the reset. Step 2 takes all sixteen producer entries; an unregistered one has an empty queue. Step 3 walks every producer's queue, not only the one that set the flag. A thread's name record and its drop lines are records in that queue, so they sit at their place. A failed append ends the pass, and the record stays at the front of its queue for the next pass. Each queue is drained to empty before the next. Step 4 copies every producer's statistics. Step 5 handles the filled image buffers of both pools. Step 6, every 5 s, checks the free space, writes the time reference and the health line, then flushes. Step 7 sums the statistics into the health and writes a fault line per changed fault counter (section 2.2). After step 7 the writer always returns to step 1. If the flag was set during the pass, that sleep ends at once, because the set is remembered. So a wake during a pass is never lost.

3. The wake: who sets the flag, what the writer does with it

Four sources set the writer's wake flag: a queue that became half full, a filled frame buffer, Destroy, and Die. The flag is a condition variable that remembers a set when nobody waits (threading.Event). The writer sleeps until the flag is set, 5 s at most. Then it resets the flag and does one pass. A set that lands during the pass stays in the flag. The next sleep ends at once, so the next pass follows without waiting. So a wake during a pass is never lost. This drawing is the answer of RCD27 (section 2.3).

4. A frame: from the shared frame buffer, through the recorder's pool, to a PNG

The pixels come from the frame buffer, a separate component (module 04): one shared-memory block of 12 slots. The frame source thread writes it. A vision job holds its latest slot. The SAM3 server process reads the same slot through the descriptor it inherited, and its reply brings the masks into the job's memory. RecordFrame copies the pixels from the held slot into a buffer of the recorder's own pool, in the app's memory. Then the job releases the shared slot. The copy exists so that no shared slot is held while the writer encodes for 40 ms. The pool is a buffer pool with a free list and a work queue, each under its own lock. Up to eight jobs produce; the writer alone consumes. The record queues of drawing 1 are different: one producer each, no lock. The writer peeks the oldest filled buffer, encodes the PNG once, and appends the frame line. Only then it dequeues the buffer and returns it to the free list. A failed append leaves the buffer at the front; the next pass skips the encode (section 2.4).

5. The lifetime: Create, Destroy, FlushInDie

Create makes the file exclusively, writes the header, makes the pools, and starts the writer. Destroy and FlushInDie share one stop request under the state lock: the reason, the deadline, then STOPPING; then the flag. Destroy waits for 'stopped' up to its timeout, then joins. FlushInDie waits for 'stopped' until its deadline. It never joins. On the writer's own thread it returns at once. The writer's last pass drains every queue and every work queue to empty, or to the deadline. What the deadline cut off is counted into the health. Then it writes the die line if a reason is set, the sums and the fault lines, the time reference and the health line, and flushes. Then it sets STOPPED and signals 'stopped'. A record call after the stop request is dropped and counted (sections 2.6, 2.7, 2.9).

6. The health: who counts what, who reads it

Every thread counts what it queued and what was dropped in its own statistics, with no lock. The writer copies every producer's statistics each pass and sums them into the health, beside its own counters. When a counter changed, it writes a fault line. The writer adds its own counters: lines, bytes, failed appends, PNGs, PNG failures, name clashes, flushes. The writer stores the free space and the under-reserve flag every 5 s. The main thread loads every counter each frame and fills the status row. Writer stalled means a filled image buffer has waited on a work queue for more than 5 s. The pool answers the oldest buffer's copy time from its own work queue (sections 2.5, 2.8).
